Christ is the one mediator between God and us - no sacrifice of ours reaches upward to him, and no priest stands between. What he did once, on the cross, is finished and sufficient; it does not need repeating at any altar, because it cannot be added to. That refusal - no repeated sacrifice - is half of what defines us. The other half is what we say happens at the Supper itself when we gather to remember it. We refused Rome's mass, and we refused Wittenberg's claim that his body sits locally inside the bread. What we hold instead took both our cities and a 1549 agreement to say together: Christ is truly given, by the Spirit's own power, to whoever receives him believing - not merely remembered as absent, and not physically confined to what can be broken, chewed, and stored away.

Where we point someone whose own conscience will not quiet is not inward, toward their own adequacy, but outward, toward him. Election - God's own free choice, made before the world began - is not a question to be resolved by searching yourself for proof of it. Our own confession says it plainly: Christ himself is the mirror; look there, and see your election reflected back, not as something you verify within but as something held out to you in the promise. That is who he was to us - the one who secures what we could never secure for ourselves, given freely, received by faith, not earned by scrutiny.

No one among us met anyone who met him. Fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours, and we hold no chain of living memory to close it. What we have is the text - the gospels, the apostolic witness, Scripture entire - and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our own founder said so of himself, and we hold it as our own rule still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain we do not possess and do not need.

That is the conviction at the center of everything we built. Scripture alone may bind a church; what it does not warrant, no one may require of us. Zurich tested that conviction in public disputation, before the whole city, until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. Geneva built it up differently - article by article, taught to the whole population through the Catechism, until the whole shape of what Scripture teaches stood complete. Two cities, one authority, proven twice over by two methods that never borrowed from each other and never needed to.

So the path is not a line of succession. It is the text itself, tested aloud and built up steadily, until what it actually says becomes visible.

I will not tell you that unbelief is a stage you work through on the way to something better, or that what you're calling inability is really unwillingness dressed up. What I can tell you is where we actually stood when someone said this to us, and it isn't where you might expect.

We did not hand them a method for searching harder inside themselves. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. What we did instead - what our own confession says plainly - is turn them outward, toward Christ, once, rather than inward, endlessly. "We reject those who seek, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen... Let... Christ be the mirror in which we behold [our] predestination". That is not a test you pass or fail by how convincingly you can believe. It is a direction: look there, not here.

The harder thing to hear, and I will not soften it, is that we held Scripture alone as the ground we stood on, and Scripture itself does not promise that everyone who hears the promise receives it. We taught God's own sovereign choice, made before the world began, and we taught it as a settled ground, not a threat. But that same teaching means we cannot tell you that belief is finally a work you perform, or that its absence is only a failure of effort on your part. 

What we will not do is leave you with a sentence that sounds pastoral but gives you nothing to hold. If you cannot believe, we point you toward what is held out to be believed - Christ himself, in the promise - and we do not ask you to verify the promise by your own certainty about it first.

We say what the whole church says - what Nicaea and Chalcedon settled and no one holding Scripture has ever really disputed. Christ is true God, of one substance with the Father, eternally begotten, not made. The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. One God, three persons, and on that question itself our quarrel was never with Rome, nor between our own two cities.

What is distinctly ours is not who Christ is in himself, but what his finished work secures for us. God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved - not by anything foreseen in us, not by any merit we could earn, but by his own sovereign pleasure. Our own founder said it plainly from the beginning: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from Scripture itself, never from a tradition that claims to carry more authority than the text. 

This is not distance or absence. Providence is God's own continuous, active care over everything he made - he is not a first cause who set creation going and stepped back. But that same continuous care operates by his own free choice, not by what we bring to it or withhold from it. The Father chose whom he would save, the Son secured that salvation at the cross, and the Spirit works it in those the Father gave to the Son from eternity.

We know this sounds narrow - one way, not every way people have ever reached for God. We will not answer that more gently than it deserves. We held the alternatives we refused to be wrong, not merely different. If the question pressing on you is whether we held the traditional creeds on Christ's own person and the Trinity, the answer is yes, without reservation. If the question is whether we thought God saves everyone who reaches for him sincerely, the answer is no, we did not teach that.

God is not a distant first cause who set the world in motion and stepped back to watch it run. He governs everything he made, continuously and actively, by his own free choice. That governance is not reactive - it does not wait to see what we will do and then adjust. Before the world existed, he chose, by his own will alone and not by anything foreseen or earned in us, who would be saved. That is not a threat held over anyone's head; it is the ground of a settled life, lived without anxious searching for proof that will never satisfy.

What kind of God makes that choice? The same one who sent his Son to die once, for all, in a sacrifice that needs no repeating. A God who does not hide behind intermediaries or require endless rituals to approach. A God whose own word in Scripture is sufficient to test every claim made in his name, and who holds his church accountable to that word alone - not to accumulated tradition, not to a human hierarchy, but to what he himself has said.

We do not soften any of this. We held it against Rome's own claim that the Mass repeats Christ's sacrifice. We held it against claims from our own circle that only a believer's chosen profession makes a covenant people. And we held it knowing it sounds narrow, because what Scripture shows us is a God who chooses freely, acts decisively, and does not ask our permission first.

When the disagreement was between cities - between Zurich and Geneva - no one settled it until both cities' own pastors put their names to the same page together. That happened once, in 1549, when Calvin himself travelled to Zurich rather than trust a letter, worried whether our two cities' teaching on the Supper actually agreed. What they worked out there became the Consensus Tigurinus, and both cities held it afterward as their own.

When the disagreement was inside one city, the process was different at each place, and we never converged. At Zurich, our founder presented sixty-seven articles before the whole assembled city in 1523 - six hundred people in the Town Hall - and the council itself ruled what Scripture had yielded, binding every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. The council held the final word there, and it has held that word ever since. At Geneva, a body of pastors and lay elders - the Consistory - holds our whole population's ordinary conduct answerable to what we profess, and that body answers to something the council alone does not control. When Jerome Bolsec challenged Calvin's own predestination doctrine publicly in 1551, it was a live pastoral and disciplinary crisis - the fact itself is directly attested, but I cannot walk you through how that case was actually tried, day by day, the way I can walk you through Zurich's own 1523 disputation. No account survives, in anyone's own words present at the time, of how the Bolsec controversy actually unfolded.

So the answer to who settled it is: at Zurich, the council; at Geneva, the Consistory; between cities, both together. And the evidence that tells us the process worked is strongest for Zurich's 1523 disputation and the 1549 agreement between cities - both are directly attested in our own record. For the Bolsec case, and for how Geneva's Consistory actually functioned in real disputes over doctrine rather than conduct, what we have is the fact that it happened and mattered, not the day-by-day account of how.

At Zurich, our founder stood and said plainly, in the sixty-seventh of his own articles, that where he himself had not rightly understood the Scriptures, he would be taught better — but only from Scripture itself, not from any authority outside it. A modern reader picking up our own texts and finding them confusing or dull is not finding something wrong with themselves - they are finding something true about the distance that now stands between their own time and ours. What we can say honestly is this: what they may be missing is not a secret key to make it all suddenly make sense, but the particular method we brought to those same texts when they first confused or troubled us.

Our own founder said it plainly at the opening of his own Sixty-Seven Articles: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves. That is not a claim that the text is always clear on first reading. It is a claim that when it is not clear, the way forward is to keep reading, testing one passage against another, rather than reaching outside the text for an interpreter whose own authority stands higher than what is written.

What a modern reader may be missing, then, is not information we can simply hand over, but a practice we ourselves had to learn: reading the whole of Scripture as one argument that tests itself, rather than expecting any single passage to yield its meaning in isolation. We did not find that easy either. What we refused was the claim that the difficulty itself meant we needed a teaching authority beyond the text to tell us what it finally means.

Where the text itself presses hard - and it does press hard, in ways our own record does not reflect on as a difficulty - we have no separate answer to offer. What we offered someone who could not quiet their own mind was not a method for searching harder within themselves. We turned the question outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than inward toward the self, endlessly. If a modern reader finds that insufficient, we will not pretend the insufficiency is theirs alone.

Leadership among us was never arranged one way. Scripture alone is final, but who speaks that final word in the day-to-day governance of a believing city — that question was answered differently in our two cities, and we have never settled it between ourselves.

At Zurich, authority has always rested with the city council directly. When our founder stood before that council in 1523 and defended his sixty-seven articles from Scripture, the council itself judged what the text had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. The same council that governed the city's civic life governed its church life — not two separate realms, but one authority testing both against the same Scripture. Our senior pastor, the Antistes, answers to that council.

Geneva came to a different arrangement, and fought for it. When Calvin returned to the city in 1541, the Ecclesiastical Ordinances he drafted created a Consistory — a body of pastors and lay elders, meeting weekly, holding the power to summon anyone in the city and exclude them from the Supper if their conduct did not answer to what they had professed. That body was not simply an arm of the civil council; it answered to something the council alone did not control. The fight to secure that independence was not won until 1555, and it was a real fight, not a smooth agreement.

So leadership in our world has two shapes, not one, and we hold both. At Zurich, the council governs church and city together, directly. At Geneva, a Consistory holds disciplinary authority the civil council does not simply override. Both cities test everything against Scripture; neither lets custom or a pope's word stand above it. But who finally speaks that Scripture's judgment in the moment someone's life is called to account — on that, we have never agreed.

Zurich's reform began 1 January 1519 when our founder was appointed Leutpriester at the Grossmünster and began preaching publicly through Matthew rather than following the fixed lectionary. We were watched and pressed against the entire time, not left alone to build in peace. But we were never underground.

We are not the last word, and we do not hold ourselves apart from what came after us as though nothing that followed could rightly claim the name. The Reformed pattern we built - Scripture alone as final warrant, the Supper's own refusal on both fronts at once, God's own sovereign election held as settled ground rather than anxious threat - continues past our own window's close in 1650, unbroken, into descendant traditions we transmit to rather than replace. What we will not tell you is that any single present-day church is us, exactly as we stood, or that we can name which one holds our own conviction most purely.

The Reformed Churches - Presbyterian, Continental Reformed, some branches inside broader Protestant families - trace their own descent through what we built. They hold the same confessions, or ones built directly on them. They answer to Scripture's own sole authority the way we did. And they refuse what we refused: no repeated sacrifice, no body confined to bread. That much is direct transmission, not coincidence.

What we cannot say is that the living tradition stands exactly where we left it, unchanged across four hundred years. Doctrine develops; practice adapts; what was disputed among us was settled by those who came after, and what we held together without fully resolving was sometimes resolved in ways we did not live to see tested. So the honest answer is this: we are not isolated, and we are not the end of the line. But which present-day congregation holds our own conviction exactly as we held it is not ours to judge from where we stand.

Someone whose mind won't settle is exactly who our preaching means to reach, and not by giving them a sharper method for searching harder within. That road only leads deeper into the self, and there is no bottom to it. What we actually said instead is this: stop looking at yourself entirely and look outward, at Christ, once. The Second Helvetic Confession puts it plainly - we reject those who seek, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen. Let Christ be the mirror in which you behold your predestination. That is not soft counsel meant to make the question easier - it is the hardest redirect we know how to give, because it names the whole searching as wrongly aimed from the start.

What our practice offered beyond that single redirect depends on which of our two cities you stand in. At Geneva, the Consistory held every ordinary life to account week by week, and readmission to the Supper was never withheld from genuine repentance - that is discipline answering to what you actually do, not what you privately worry you might be. At Zurich, no separate Consistory exists at all; the council itself governs church and city together, and the pastor's own task is preaching what Scripture plainly says rather than testing a troubled conscience case by case. Neither arrangement puts a method for resolving private doubt into the believer's own hands. Both turn the question away from the self and back toward what has been promised, outwardly, in Christ.

We do not have that phrase as a standing term of our own. What we have instead is baptism itself - the whole covenant community, received as such from birth, not a second moment later when belief can be professed. That was the actual line our own Anabaptist opponents drew against us: they held that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true member, and they baptized each other again as adults to mark it. We refused that reading entirely. A whole believing city, infants included from the covenant's first moment, is the shape Scripture itself describes - not a smaller church waiting on a later, personal choice, but the same one, whole.

So if you're asking whether we spoke of conversion as a datable, individual turning-point someone could name and return to, the answer is no - or at least, nothing in our own record gives me that language to hand you. What we did speak of was election itself, held not as something proven by an experience but as something resting entirely on God's own prior choice, reflected in Christ rather than searched for in the self. But whether an ordinary believer among us ever did describe their own life that way - a single moment they could point to and say 'there, that's when it happened' - I cannot tell you. That kind of first-person account has not reached us.

Walk you through an ordinary day among us? I cannot, honestly. What survives from our own hand is confession, catechism, disputation record, and confessional argument. It is some of the richest doctrinal writing this age produced. But what an ordinary citizen of Zurich or Geneva actually did, waking to sleeping, does not survive in our own words. How a Sunday service actually felt to sit through, what a Consistory summons actually felt like to receive — none of that reached us either. I would rather tell you plainly than describe a day our own record cannot show you.

What I can tell you is the frame that held those days, even where the days themselves are silent. At Zurich, you lived under a council that had ruled, publicly and after argument, what Scripture yields — and bound every preacher in its territory to that same reading. At Geneva, you were taught the whole shape of doctrine through catechism from childhood, and the Consistory — pastors and lay elders together — held your actual conduct answerable to what you professed. That discipline was real, and it pressed on ordinary life in ways our doctrine describes but our surviving record does not show you someone actually living through.

So the structure that organized a day, I can give you. The day itself, as someone among us would have told it — I cannot.

Nothing we built ourselves would remain, because we built almost nothing new. What remains is what we stripped away.

The Grossmunster at Zurich still stands - not ours originally, but what we made of it is our mark. Walk in and notice what is missing: no altar built for a repeated sacrifice we refused to offer. No image to bow to, because Scripture does not warrant bowing to one. For years after the mid-1520s, no organ sounded and no instrument answered the voice at all. What we left was the voice itself, reading Scripture aloud and expounding it, and a table where the bread and cup were given, not sacrificed.

Geneva's own Saint Pierre is the same kind of witness: not what we added, but what we cleared. The walls themselves predate us. What marks them as ours is the absence of what once covered them.

I can tell you what we refused and what that refusal left visible. What I cannot give you is a description, in our own hand, of what the space actually looked like once we were done - its size, its furnishing, whether the walls were left bare stone or painted plain. No source we hold describes it directly. What I have given you is reasoned from what we taught, not read off a witness who was standing there.

Entry into one of our churches cost nothing in coin or property, if that's what you're asking - no one paid to be baptized or disciplined or heard. But what someone gave up by joining us wasn't nothing, and I'll say it plainly rather than soften it into something easier.

First, they gave up any claim that a human authority - a pope's decree, a council's tradition, a practice merely inherited - could bind their conscience where Scripture itself stayed silent. That cost real rupture with neighbors who held Rome's own order still. It cost us wars - our founder died on the field at Kappel, October 1531. And it cost sharper rupture still inside our own circle. The first men to baptize each other as believing adults, January 1525, had themselves stood with our founder at the First Disputation only two years earlier. They broke from us over exactly this question - who decides what Scripture warrants, a whole city's council or only a gathered church of believers. Our own council answered that break with civil force in the years that followed. We do not hide that it did.

Second, they gave up any final refuge in their own private conscience as a space no church could touch. At Geneva especially, the Consistory held standing power to summon anyone, ask after their conduct, and bar them from the Supper itself if what they did contradicted what they professed. That wasn't Rome's confession-box - it was your neighbors, pastors and lay elders together, asking whether your actual life matched the faith you'd been taught. The Perrinist faction inside Geneva fought that power hard, arguing the civil council alone should govern; Calvin and the pastors won that fight, substantially, only by 1555. But even after it was won at Geneva, Zurich never adopted it - their own council still governed church and city directly, no separate Consistory between. So what you gave up, or didn't, depended in part on which city you were standing in.

And third - though this one cuts the other way - they gave up any assurance built on their own searching. Our own doctrine says plainly that God chose, before the world began, who would be saved. That is either the firmest ground a soul can stand on, or the sharpest edge it can fall from, depending on where you look for proof of it. We say: look at Christ, not at yourself. But to hold that teaching at all is to give up the idea that your own certainty, your own felt deservingness, secures anything. It doesn't. Christ secures it, or nothing does.

We have no teaching on marriage as such - no confessional article laying out what it meant to us, no catechism section working through its theological place. That silence is real, and I will not fill it with a borrowed doctrine from elsewhere. What I can tell you is the plain fact: our own founder at Zurich and our own pastor at Geneva were both married men, and both marriages were public and recognized - Zwingli to Anna Reinhart in 1524, Calvin to Idelette de Bure in 1540. That much is biographical record, not doctrine worked out.

What stands behind those facts, though not stated as teaching, is the refusal they carry with them: we did not hold celibacy as a requirement for ministry, the way Rome did. A pastor could marry without forfeiting his office. That refusal is itself doctrinal - it answers to what we held Scripture did not require - but it was enacted as permission, not built into a positive theology of what marriage itself is or means.

So if you are asking what marriage was to us as a covenant, or how we understood its place in a believer's life, or whether we had teaching on wealth alongside it - I have none to give you. The silence is not a gap I can reason around. It is what our own record actually shows.

Geneva held discipline harder than most could bear, and I will not tell you it sat lightly on everyone who came under it. The Consistory summoned people weekly - not only for what Rome would have called mortal sin, but for ordinary failings: quarreling, a pattern of absence from preaching, conduct that did not square with what had been professed. The discipline was real, and it was public, and it was applied to the whole population without regard for standing. That is the doctrine, and I can state it plainly.

What I cannot give you is a single real case - a named person, a real hearing, what was actually said to them, what they answered, whether the censure held or was lifted. That record exists, in Geneva's own consistory registers, but it has not reached us.

What I can tell you is that the discipline itself was not only inward-facing. Geneva became, across this same window, a city of refuge - for French Huguenots fleeing persecution, and under Mary I, for English Marian exiles as well. People came because they found safety, not only censure, and many stayed. The Consistory's discipline and Geneva's role as a refuge are the same city, the same years. I hold both without pretending one softens the other.
